name: Auguste Comte
summary: French philosopher who coined the word sociology and held that society should be studied by the positive methods of the natural sciences.

name: Karl Marx
summary: German thinker whose historical materialism explains society through its mode of production and the struggle between classes.

name: Friedrich Engels
summary: Marx's lifelong collaborator and co-author of The Communist Manifesto, who traced the family and the state to private property.

name: Émile Durkheim
summary: French founder of academic sociology who treated social facts as things and explained social order through solidarity and the collective conscience.

name: Max Weber
summary: German sociologist of interpretive understanding who studied social action, authority, bureaucracy and the part religion played in the rise of capitalism.

name: Talcott Parsons
summary: American structural functionalist who built a general theory of action and of society as a social system.

name: Robert K. Merton
summary: American functionalist who refined functional analysis and proposed middle-range theory, reference group theory and a structural theory of deviance.

name: George Herbert Mead
summary: American pragmatist philosopher whose account of the self, symbols and role-taking became the basis of symbolic interactionism.

name: Charles Horton Cooley
summary: American sociologist who described the looking-glass self and the primary group.

name: Herbert Blumer
summary: American sociologist, a student of Mead, who named and systematised symbolic interactionism.

name: Erving Goffman
summary: Canadian-born American sociologist who analysed face-to-face interaction through the dramaturgical metaphor of performance.

name: C. Wright Mills
aliases: Charles Wright Mills|C.W. Mills|C Wright Mills
summary: American critical sociologist who wrote on the sociological imagination and on the power elite in the United States.

name: Bronisław Malinowski
summary: Polish-born British anthropologist who pioneered long-term fieldwork and participant observation in the Trobriand Islands.

name: Claude Lévi-Strauss
summary: French structural anthropologist whose alliance theory explains kinship through marriage exchange between groups.

name: George Peter Murdock
summary: American anthropologist whose cross-cultural survey in Social Structure (1949) argued that the nuclear family is universal.

name: Kingsley Davis
summary: American sociologist and demographer who, with Wilbert Moore, proposed the functionalist theory of stratification.

name: Pitirim Sorokin
summary: Russian-American sociologist whose Social Mobility (1927) was the first systematic study of movement between social positions.

name: Vilfredo Pareto
summary: Italian economist and sociologist of elite theory, known for the circulation of elites.

name: Robert Michels
summary: German-born sociologist whose study of socialist parties led to the iron law of oligarchy.

name: T.H. Marshall
summary: British sociologist who traced the growth of citizenship from civil to political to social rights.

name: Thomas Robert Malthus
summary: English clergyman and economist who argued that population tends to grow faster than the means of subsistence.

name: William F. Ogburn
summary: American sociologist who studied technology and social change and introduced the idea of cultural lag.

name: Andre Gunder Frank
summary: German-born economic historian and sociologist of dependency theory who argued that capitalism produced Latin American underdevelopment.

name: Harry Braverman
summary: American Marxist writer who argued that monopoly capitalism degrades work by deskilling it.

name: G.S. Ghurye
summary: Pioneer of Indian sociology at Bombay University who studied caste, tribes and Indian culture through an Indological approach.

name: M.N. Srinivas
summary: Indian sociologist of the structural-functional and field-view approach who introduced Sanskritisation, Westernisation and dominant caste.

name: A.R. Desai
summary: Indian Marxist sociologist who analysed nationalism, peasant struggles and the post-colonial state in class terms.

name: Louis Dumont
summary: French anthropologist who explained caste as a hierarchy grounded in the religious opposition of pure and impure.

name: André Béteille
summary: Indian sociologist who studied caste, class and power in a Tanjore village and the growing separation of these dimensions of inequality.

name: Yogendra Singh
summary: Indian sociologist who analysed the modernisation of Indian tradition as cultural and structural, orthogenetic and heterogenetic change.

name: Irawati Karve
summary: Indian anthropologist who mapped kinship organisation in India into regional zones.

name: S.C. Dube
summary: Indian anthropologist whose study of Shamirpet near Hyderabad was among the first Indian village monographs.

name: Robert Redfield
summary: American anthropologist of peasant society who distinguished the great tradition and the little tradition of a civilisation.

name: McKim Marriott
summary: American anthropologist whose study of Kishan Garhi village described universalisation and parochialisation.

name: Milton Singer
summary: American anthropologist who studied how Madras industrial leaders kept up Hindu tradition alongside modern industrial work.

name: Daniel Thorner
summary: American economic historian of India who classified agrarian classes as malik, kisan and mazdur.

name: Verrier Elwin
summary: British-born anthropologist of central Indian tribes who urged their protection from outside exploitation and later advised Nehru on tribal policy.

name: N.K. Bose
summary: Indian anthropologist who described how tribes were absorbed into Hindu society as castes.

name: B.R. Ambedkar
aliases: Ambedkar|B. R. Ambedkar|Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar|Babasaheb Ambedkar
summary: Dalit leader, jurist and chair of the Constitution's Drafting Committee, who argued for the annihilation of caste.

name: Rajni Kothari
summary: Indian political scientist who analysed the Congress system of one-party dominance and the politicisation of caste.

name: A.M. Shah
summary: Indian sociologist who studied the household as a dimension of the family in India.

name: Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844
summary: Marx's early writings on the alienation of the worker from the product, the labour process, species-being and other people.
note: Written in 1844; first published in full in 1932.

name: The Communist Manifesto
aliases: Communist Manifesto|Manifesto of the Communist Party
summary: Pamphlet declaring that the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.
note: Co-written with Engels.

name: Capital, Volume I
summary: Marx's analysis of capitalist production, showing how capital extracts surplus value from wage labour.
note: Volumes II (1885) and III (1894) were edited by Engels and published after Marx's death.

name: The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State
summary: Links the rise of the monogamous family and the state to private property, drawing on Lewis Henry Morgan's Ancient Society.

name: The Division of Labour in Society
aliases: Division of Labour|The Division of Labor in Society|De la division du travail social
summary: Argues that society moves from mechanical solidarity based on likeness to organic solidarity based on specialised interdependence.

name: The Rules of Sociological Method
summary: Durkheim's statement of method: treat social facts as things and explain them by other social facts.

name: Suicide
aliases: Suicide: A Study in Sociology|Le Suicide
summary: Uses suicide rates to show how integration and regulation shape suicide, distinguishing egoistic, altruistic, anomic and fatalistic types.

name: The Elementary Forms of the Religious Life
aliases: The Elementary Forms of Religious Life|Elementary Forms
summary: Studies Australian Aboriginal totemism to argue that religion separates sacred from profane and that its real object is society itself.

name: The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism
aliases: Protestant Ethic|Die protestantische Ethik und der Geist des Kapitalismus
summary: Argues that Calvinist ideas of calling and predestination fostered the disciplined, rational conduct suited to modern capitalism.
note: Published as two essays in 1904-05 and revised in 1920; Talcott Parsons' English translation appeared in 1930.

name: Economy and Society
summary: Weber's unfinished treatise on social action, legitimate authority, bureaucracy, and class, status and party.
note: Published after his death by Marianne Weber in 1921-22; full English edition 1968.

name: The Religion of India
aliases: The Religion of India: The Sociology of Hinduism and Buddhism|Hinduismus und Buddhismus
summary: Weber's study of Hinduism and Buddhism, arguing that caste and the doctrines of karma and dharma did not favour a rational capitalist ethic.
note: German essays 1916-17; English translation 1958.

name: The Structure of Social Action
summary: Draws on Marshall, Pareto, Durkheim and Weber to build a voluntaristic theory of action.

name: The Social System
summary: Treats society as a system of interrelated parts held together by shared values, institutionalised roles and socialisation.

name: Social Theory and Social Structure
summary: Merton's collection on functional analysis, middle-range theory, reference groups and deviance.
note: Enlarged editions appeared in 1957 and 1968.

name: Social Structure and Anomie
summary: Article arguing that deviance arises when a culture stresses success goals but the social structure limits the legitimate means to reach them.

name: Mind, Self and Society
summary: Lectures on how mind and self arise in social interaction through language, role-taking and the generalised other.
note: Published after Mead's death from students' notes, edited by Charles W. Morris.

name: The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life
summary: Analyses everyday interaction as a performance with front and back regions and impression management.
note: First published in 1956 in Edinburgh; the widely cited US edition is 1959.

name: The Sociological Imagination
summary: Calls for a sociology that links personal troubles to public issues of social structure and history.

name: The Power Elite
summary: Argues that interlocking corporate, military and political elites hold power in the United States.

name: Some Principles of Stratification
summary: Argues that stratification is functionally necessary, as unequal rewards draw the ablest people into the most important positions.
note: Co-written with Wilbert E. Moore; criticised by Melvin Tumin in 1953.

name: An Essay on the Principle of Population
aliases: Essay on the Principle of Population|Malthusian theory
summary: Argues that population grows geometrically while subsistence grows arithmetically, so positive and preventive checks hold population down.

name: The Development of Underdevelopment
summary: Essay arguing that Latin American underdevelopment results from the satellite's exploitative ties to the capitalist metropolis.

name: Caste and Race in India
summary: Ghurye's study of caste, setting out its six features and tracing it to Brahmanic Indo-Aryan culture in the Gangetic plain.

name: The Aborigines—So-called—and Their Future
aliases: The Aborigines So-called and Their Future|The Scheduled Tribes|Backward Hindus
summary: Argues that Indian tribes are backward Hindus who should be integrated into Hindu society, not isolated.
note: Later editions were titled The Scheduled Tribes.

name: Religion and Society among the Coorgs of South India
aliases: Religion and Society Among the Coorgs|Coorgs
summary: Study of Coorg religion and ritual in which Srinivas introduced the concept of Sanskritisation.

name: Social Change in Modern India
summary: Srinivas's lectures on Sanskritisation, Westernisation and secularisation as processes of change in Indian society.

name: Social Background of Indian Nationalism
aliases: The Social Background of Indian Nationalism
summary: Marxist account of how British rule transformed India's economy and classes and so gave rise to Indian nationalism.

name: Homo Hierarchicus
aliases: Homo Hierarchicus: The Caste System and Its Implications
summary: Argues that caste rests on hierarchy grounded in the opposition of pure and impure, with status encompassing power.
note: French original 1966; English translation 1970.

name: Caste, Class and Power
summary: Study of Sripuram, a Tanjore village, showing caste, class and power growing apart as bases of stratification.

name: Modernization of Indian Tradition
summary: Analyses change in Indian society as orthogenetic and heterogenetic change in its cultural tradition and social structure.

name: Kinship Organisation in India
summary: Karve's survey dividing Indian kinship into northern, central, southern and eastern zones.

name: Indian Village
summary: Monograph on Shamirpet village near Hyderabad describing its caste, family, economy, ritual and change.

name: Peasant Society and Culture
summary: Treats peasant society as a part-society linked to a wider civilisation through its great and little traditions.

name: When a Great Tradition Modernizes
summary: Study of Madras showing industrial leaders adapting Hindu tradition to modern industry rather than abandoning it.

name: The Agrarian Prospect in India
aliases: Agrarian Prospect in India|Malik kisan mazdur
summary: Thorner's lectures on India's agrarian structure, dividing rural classes into malik, kisan and mazdur.

name: Annihilation of Caste
summary: Argues that caste cannot be reformed and must be destroyed by rejecting the religious scriptures that sanction it.
note: Written as a speech for the Jat-Pat Todak Mandal of Lahore, which cancelled the event; Ambedkar published it himself.

name: The Household Dimension of the Family in India
summary: Argues that the household must be studied apart from the wider family and traces how Indian households change over time.
note: Editions dated 1973 and 1974 are both cited.

name: Positivism
summary: The view that society should be studied, like nature, through observation, comparison and experiment to discover its laws.

name: Law of three stages
summary: Comte's law that human thought, and society with it, passes through theological, metaphysical and positive stages.

name: Historical materialism
aliases: Materialist conception of history|Mode of production|Forces and relations of production
summary: Marx's view that the mode of production, combining forces and relations of production, shapes society and drives historical change.

name: Base and superstructure
summary: Marx's model in which the economic base of production relations conditions the legal, political and ideological superstructure.

name: Alienation
summary: Under capitalism the worker is estranged from the product, the act of production, human species-being and other people.

name: Class struggle
summary: Conflict between classes defined by ownership of the means of production; a class-in-itself becomes a class-for-itself through shared consciousness.

name: Surplus value
summary: The value workers create beyond the value of their wages, taken by the capitalist as the source of profit.

name: False consciousness
summary: Beliefs that hide real class relations and exploitation from those who are subordinated.
note: The phrase is Engels's, from his 1893 letter to Franz Mehring; Marx never used it, though it is often credited to him.

name: Social fact
summary: Ways of acting, thinking and feeling that are external to individuals and exercise constraint over them; to be treated as things.

name: Mechanical and organic solidarity
summary: Mechanical solidarity binds similar people through a strong collective conscience; organic solidarity binds specialised, interdependent people through the division of labour.

name: Collective conscience
summary: The totality of beliefs and sentiments common to average members of a society, forming a system with a life of its own.

name: Anomie
summary: A state of deregulation in which social norms fail to limit individual desires, seen in anomic suicide and the anomic division of labour.
note: Durkheim's concept; Merton later recast it as a gap between cultural goals and legitimate means.

name: Sacred and profane
summary: Durkheim's division of things into the sacred, set apart and forbidden, and the profane; religion unites believers around sacred things.

name: Verstehen
summary: Weber's method of understanding social action by grasping the subjective meanings actors attach to it.

name: Ideal type
summary: An analytical construct that one-sidedly accentuates features of reality, used to compare actual cases; neither a moral ideal nor an average.

name: Social action
summary: Action oriented to the behaviour of others; Weber's four types are instrumentally rational, value-rational, affectual and traditional action.

name: Types of authority
summary: Weber's three bases of legitimate domination: traditional, charismatic and legal-rational authority.

name: Bureaucracy
summary: Weber's ideal type of legal-rational administration: hierarchy, written rules, impersonality, specialised trained officials and salaried careers.

name: Rationalisation
summary: The spread of calculable, rule-governed and efficient action in modern life, which brings the disenchantment of the world.
note: The phrase 'iron cage' is Parsons' 1930 translation of Weber's 'stahlhartes Gehäuse'.

name: Value neutrality
summary: Weber's principle that values may guide the choice of topic but personal value judgements must be kept out of scientific analysis.

name: Class, status and party
summary: Weber's three dimensions of the distribution of power: class (market situation), status (social honour and lifestyle) and party (political organisation).

name: AGIL scheme
summary: Parsons' four problems every social system must solve: adaptation, goal attainment, integration and latency, or pattern maintenance.

name: Pattern variables
summary: Five pairs of choices that orient action, such as affectivity versus affective neutrality and universalism versus particularism.

name: Manifest and latent functions
summary: Manifest functions are intended and recognised consequences of a social item; latent functions are neither intended nor recognised.

name: Dysfunction
summary: Merton's term for consequences of a social item that lessen the adaptation or adjustment of a system.

name: Theories of the middle range
summary: Merton's call for theories between minor working hypotheses and all-inclusive grand theory, closely tied to empirical research.

name: Reference group
summary: A group whose standards people use to judge themselves, including non-membership groups that lead to anticipatory socialisation.
note: Herbert Hyman coined the term in 1942; Merton developed reference group theory.

name: Relative deprivation
summary: A sense of deprivation that comes from comparison with a reference group rather than from absolute conditions.
note: The concept comes from Stouffer's The American Soldier (1949); Merton and Kitt developed it.

name: Strain theory
aliases: Modes of individual adaptation|Anomie theory of deviance
summary: Deviance arises when culture stresses success goals but limits legitimate means; adaptations are conformity, innovation, ritualism, retreatism and rebellion.

name: Self-fulfilling prophecy
summary: A false definition of a situation that evokes new behaviour which makes the originally false conception come true.
note: Merton coined the term in 1948, building on the Thomas theorem.

name: The self (I and me)
aliases: I and me|The I and the me|Play stage|Game stage
summary: Mead's self arises in social interaction; the 'I' is its spontaneous response and the 'me' the attitudes of others it has taken in.

name: Generalised other
summary: The organised attitudes of the whole community, which a person takes into account in the game stage.

name: Looking-glass self
summary: Cooley's idea that the self grows from imagining how we appear to others, how they judge us, and the feeling that results.

name: Symbolic interactionism
summary: Perspective holding that people act on meanings that arise in social interaction and are handled through interpretation.
note: Blumer coined the term in 1937; the ideas are largely Mead's, but Mead did not use it.

name: Dramaturgy
summary: Goffman's view of interaction as a performance in which people manage the impressions they give to others.

name: Participant observation
summary: Fieldwork method in which the researcher lives among the people studied and takes part in their daily life.

name: Alliance theory
aliases: Exchange of women|The Elementary Structures of Kinship
summary: Lévi-Strauss's theory that kinship rests on marriage alliances between groups, created by the exchange of women under the incest taboo.

name: Universality of the nuclear family
summary: Murdock's claim that the nuclear family is universal and performs sexual, economic, reproductive and educational functions.

name: Vertical and horizontal mobility
summary: Sorokin's distinction between movement up or down the social hierarchy and movement between positions at the same level.

name: Circulation of elites
summary: Pareto's theory that history is a succession of elites, with lion-like and fox-like elites replacing one another.

name: Iron law of oligarchy
summary: Michels's law that every large organisation, even a democratic party, comes to be ruled by a small leadership.
note: Set out in Political Parties: German original 1911, English translation 1915.

name: Citizenship rights
summary: Marshall's account of citizenship in Britain expanding from civil rights to political rights and then to social rights.

name: Cultural lag
summary: Ogburn's idea that non-material culture adapts more slowly than material culture and technology, creating strain.

name: Dependency theory
summary: The view that poor countries are underdeveloped because of their exploitative dependence on the developed capitalist core.

name: Deskilling
summary: Braverman's thesis, in Labor and Monopoly Capital, that monopoly capitalism separates conception from execution and strips workers of skill.

name: Ghurye's six features of caste
aliases: Features of caste|Six features of caste
summary: Segmental division, hierarchy, restrictions on feeding and social intercourse, civil and religious disabilities, restricted choice of occupation, and endogamy.

name: Sanskritisation
summary: Process by which a low caste or tribe adopts the customs, rituals and way of life of a higher, often twice-born, caste to claim higher status.
note: Introduced in the Coorgs study (1952); Srinivas first called it Brahminisation.

name: Westernisation
summary: Srinivas's term for changes in Indian society and culture from over 150 years of British rule, in technology, institutions, ideology and values.

name: Dominant caste
summary: A caste that dominates a village through numerical strength and economic and political power, helped by a ritual rank that is not too low.

name: Vote bank
summary: A bloc of voters, often of one caste or community, delivered to a party through leaders who promise it benefits.

name: Purity and pollution
aliases: Pure and impure|Opposition of pure and impure
summary: Dumont's principle that caste hierarchy rests on the opposition of pure and impure, placing the Brahmin at the top and the untouchable at the bottom.

name: Great and little traditions
summary: Redfield's distinction between the great tradition of the reflective few, carried in texts and temples, and the little tradition of the unreflective many in villages.

name: Universalisation and parochialisation
summary: Marriott's two processes: little-tradition elements rise into the great tradition, and great-tradition elements are taken into local practice.

name: Compartmentalisation
summary: Singer's term for how Madras industrialists kept modern work and traditional ritual life in separate spheres.

name: Isolationist approach to tribes
summary: Elwin's early proposal to protect tribal areas from outside contact and exploitation, often called the national park approach.
note: Elwin later moved towards integration as adviser for NEFA.

name: Hindu method of tribal absorption
summary: Bose's account of how tribes entered Hindu society as castes, drawn by the economic security of the caste division of labour.

name: Congress system
summary: Kothari's term for the Congress-dominated party system, in which opposition parties worked as parties of pressure on its margins.

name: Jajmani system
summary: Hereditary exchange in which service castes serve landowning patron families in return for grain and other customary payments.
note: First analysed as a system in W.H. Wiser's The Hindu Jajmani System (1936).

name: Demographic transition theory
summary: Theory that populations move from high birth and death rates, through falling death rates, to low birth and death rates.
note: Associated with Warren Thompson (1929) and Frank Notestein (1945).

name: Tribal Panchsheel
aliases: Panchsheel for tribal development|Nehru's Panchsheel for tribals
summary: Nehru's five principles for tribal policy, stressing development along tribes' own genius, land and forest rights, and tribal self-administration.
note: Set out in Nehru's foreword to Elwin's A Philosophy for NEFA; not the 1954 India-China Panchsheel.

name: French Revolution
summary: Overthrow of the French monarchy which, with the Industrial Revolution, raised the problems of order and change from which sociology emerged.

name: First Census of India
summary: The first all-India census, taken region by region at different times rather than on one date.
note: Not synchronous; the first synchronous census was held in 1881.

name: Constitution of India comes into force
summary: The Constitution came into force and India became a republic committed to justice, liberty, equality and fraternity.
note: Adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 26 November 1949.

name: Community Development Programme
summary: Programme of all-round rural development, launched in selected areas, to improve farming, health, education and welfare through people's participation.

name: Balwantrai Mehta Committee
summary: Committee that reviewed the Community Development Programme and recommended three-tier Panchayati Raj as democratic decentralisation.

name: National Family Planning Programme
summary: India became the first country to start a national family planning programme.

name: Mandal Commission
summary: Commission under B.P. Mandal that identified Other Backward Classes and recommended 27 per cent reservation for them.
note: Set up in 1979, reported in 1980; the V.P. Singh government decided to implement it in 1990.

name: 73rd Constitutional Amendment
summary: Gave constitutional status to three-tier Panchayati Raj, with one-third of seats reserved for women and reservation for SCs and STs.
note: Passed in 1992; came into force on 24 April 1993.

name: Chipko movement
summary: Villagers in the Garhwal Himalaya, many of them women, hugged trees to stop the commercial felling of their forests.

name: National Population Policy 2000
summary: Set replacement-level fertility as the medium-term goal and a stable population by 2045 as the long-term goal.
